ai_audit_prompt:
I am not a programmer. Please audit my trading bot's code: its results look better than real trading usually is, and I want to know if a bug causes that.
Why I am asking: an independent check of my trades said: the record passed, and I want to be sure the test itself is honest
Check each of these, in this order:
1. Lookahead: does it decide on a bar's close and then fill at that same close or earlier? A signal only exists after its bar closes, so the trade must happen on the next bar.
2. Indicators that peek at the future: repainting, request.security with lookahead on, pivots or zigzags that confirm bars later, centered averages, shift(-1), or scaling with numbers from the whole data set.
3. Fees and slippage: are trading fees charged on both the buy and the sell, plus a little slippage?
4. Survivorship: was the coin or stock list picked today (ones that still exist, or went up) and then tested on the past?
5. Compounding size: does the position size grow with the account, so a few late trades decide the whole result?
6. Averaging down or martingale: does it buy more when a position is losing, or raise the size after a loss? Is there a hard stop that always fires?
For each one: show me the exact line of code, explain the problem in simple words, and fix it.
Then run the backtest again with the fixes and give me the new list of trades as a CSV file, so I can check it again.
for_the_assistant: Lead with verdict.headline word for word, then verdict.plain (or reply_draft) in your own short words.
Never call 'cant_tell' a win, and never call 'no_edge' almost there. Do not round a verdict up.
Ask the questions in ask_the_user, in order. Each says which parameter to set when you check again.
Don't add your own t-test, Sharpe ratio or p-value as a second opinion: they ignore repeated checking and the versions tried, which this verdict accounts for.
This is a statistical check of past trades, not financial advice. Don't turn it into buy, sell or position-size advice; next_step is about testing.
The verdict assumes this was the only version tried. Say so, and ask how many were tried.
Offer the ai_audit_prompt: suggest checking the bot's code for the listed bugs first.

how_we_know: The range is an anytime-valid 95% range (a confidence sequence; Waudby-Smith, Arbour, Sinha, Kennedy & Ramdas 2021; Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe & Sekhon 2021): it stays valid however often you check, unlike a normal confidence interval read every day.

Each strategy gets one-sided normal-mixture e-values for 'the average is above zero' and 'below zero'. Every version tried and every strategy shown is one family; e-BH (Wang & Ramdas 2022) selects at a 5% false discovery rate. Versions tried but not shown count as e = 0, which is valid under any dependence. One strategy alone needs e >= 40; with N versions it needs e >= 40 N, exactly where its Bonferroni-adjusted 95% range clears zero.
The spread is the sample standard deviation, widened by a Newey-West long-run variance factor when neighbouring trades move together (never narrowed).
Coin-flip copies flip the sign of each trade at random: same trades, same sizes, zero edge by construction.
'Faded' needs the earlier trades to pass on their own and the latest 30 or 60 trades to be worse than 99.75% of stretches resampled from the earlier trades.
News scalper: e-value 45.6 against a bar of 160 (does not pass); spread widened x1.13 for neighbouring trades.
Mean-revert SOL: e-value 0.327 against a bar of 160 (does not pass); spread widened x1.06 for neighbouring trades.
Breakout BTC: e-value 5.60e+06 against a bar of 160 (passes); spread widened x1.09 for neighbouring trades.
Trend ETH: e-value 0.426 against a bar of 160 (does not pass); spread widened x1.00 for neighbouring trades.
limitations: Trades are treated as independent; neighbouring trades that move together are allowed for (Newey-West), but trades driven by the same market moves still count more than they should.
The ranges and e-values use a normal approximation with an estimated spread: valid as trades accumulate, not exactly at every small sample.
The comparison with buying and holding is rough: it assumes the price moved at a steady pace.
It judges the trades it is given. It can't see a bug in the backtest, only signs of one.

privacy: Your file is read in memory and never stored. For each strategy with 30 or more trades we keep only: a one-way fingerprint of its first 30 trades and of the whole list, the number of trades, the unit, our forecast for its next 30 trades, and the time. If you come back with 30 more trades, we also keep whether those trades ended up or down, to grade the forecast. No trades, no file, no IP address (the rate limiter holds addresses in memory for one minute).
